name: Fabricated Citations and Fact Checking
title: Fabricated Citations and Fact Checking
answer: Fabricated citations are references that appear in a manuscript but do not correspond to a real publication, or that misrepresent a real work's authors, title, venue, year, or findings. They arise from language models that generate plausible-looking bibliographies, from citation padding, and from careless copying between papers. Fact checking in this context means verifying that each cited work exists, that its metadata is accurate, and that the cited claim is actually supported by the source. The topic sits in governance, ethics, and research integrity because fabricated citations can distort the scholarly record, mislead readers, and hide the absence of evidence. The scale is large: this site alone holds 135 research papers and 12026 claims extracted from research works, which shows why automated assistance and human review are both needed.

sections.body: Fabricated citations are references that appear in a manuscript but do not correspond to a real publication, or that misrepresent a real work's authors, title, venue, year, or findings. They arise from language models that generate plausible-looking bibliographies, from citation padding, and from careless copying between papers. Fact checking in this context means verifying that each cited work exists, that its metadata is accurate, and that the cited claim is actually supported by the source. The topic sits in governance, ethics, and research integrity because fabricated citations can distort the scholarly record, mislead readers, and hide the absence of evidence. The scale is large: this site alone holds 135 research papers and 12026 claims extracted from research works, which shows why automated assistance and human review are both needed.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Fact checking runs on access to authoritative bibliographic records, publisher pages, digital object identifiers, library catalogues, and retraction notices. It also depends on the full text of the cited work, not just an abstract or a search snippet, so that a claim can be checked in context. Reference managers, plagiarism detectors, and citation graph tools can help, but they do not replace reading the source. In an AI research setting, the infrastructure may include a document store, a metadata resolver, and a review queue where uncertain citations are flagged for a person. The site's own practice of linking to the original paper rather than to the Consensus search tool reflects this need for provenance.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A fact checker starts with the citation as written, then searches for the title, author list, and venue in multiple independent sources. If the work exists, the checker compares the cited claim against the original text to see whether the source supports it, contradicts it, or is silent. For suspected fabrications, the checker looks for patterns such as missing identifiers, inconsistent metadata, or references that appear only in AI-generated text. Tools can extract references and match them against databases, but a human reviewer is needed to judge ambiguous cases and confirm the final record. The workflow ends with a correction, a retraction, or a note in the manuscript, depending on the severity and the venue's policy.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The risks include reputational damage, wasted research effort, and the erosion of trust in published work. Provenance matters because a citation is a claim about where an idea came from, and fabricated citations break that chain. Institutions and publishers may have policies on authorship, citation accuracy, and research misconduct, and these policies can trigger investigations when fabrications are found. Rights issues can arise when a citation misattributes credit or when a retracted work is cited without acknowledgement. A common practice is to keep a record of how each citation was verified, including the source consulted and the date of the check, so that the verification itself is auditable.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: As generative models become more common in drafting, fabricated citations are likely to appear more often and in more varied forms. Fact checking is moving toward a combination of automated metadata checks, claim-level verification, and human review, with provenance recorded at the point of writing. Publishers and preprint servers are experimenting with reference validation at submission, and some are requiring authors to confirm that they have read the cited works. The long term aim is not only to catch fabrications but to make the origin of every claim visible and checkable. In this atlas, the topic connects to the wider library of 91 AI books, 800 scientific models, 732 AI tools, and 686 glossary terms, because citation integrity depends on shared definitions, accessible sources, and reliable tools.
